paper_title: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

Introduction System Two reasoning has substantially advanced language model capabilities in mathematics, coding, and science [3, 23, 34, 46, 55, 62]. These gains often come at higher inference cost, as models generate additional reasoning tokens before answering [12, 27, 29, 37, 60]. Yet many routine decisions in software workflows, such as routing requests, selecting tool actions, and verifying task completion, can be made without generating explicit reasoning traces. System One models [2, 28, 64, 67, 86, 86, 95] such as Jev [2] predict distribution over predefined outcomes in single forward pass, substantially reducing inference latency and providing structured outputs that downstream software can use directly. Recent benchmarks evaluate System One models across range of decision tasks and settings [1, 5, 7, 11, 81]. Building on these evaluations, we argue that benchmark designed to characterize the capabilities and reliability of System One models should provide trustworthy reference labels supported by model-visible evidence, distinguish performance across increasing task complexity, evaluate models both as actors and verifiers in interactive settings, and assess decision reliability under controlled changes to the available options. To address these requirements, we introduce SO-Arena, benchmark comprising 2,919 tasks across eleven domains organized into five capability families: semantic understanding, knowledge and reasoning, safety and policy compliance, evidence assessment, and agent task completion. The benchmark brings together static and environment-grounded tasks under unified decision interface, with performSO-Arena ance evaluated at the level of the original task. We curate tasks from traceable sources, manually verify that reference labels are supported by the information available to the model, and keep evaluation references separate from model inputs. To characterize the capability spectrum beyond aggregate accuracy, we organize nine domains into difficulty tiers based on domain-specific criteria for task complexity. We report performance across these tiers and construct capability leaderboard that weights all eleven domains equally while emphasizing the most demanding tasks. In agentic settings, we further distinguish between action selection and completion verification. The former evaluates whether models can accomplish goals through sequential decisions in web and tool environments, while the latter assesses whether they can correctly judge recorded executions, including cases where identical final goal states conceal different compliance with intermediate requirements. We also incorporate reasoning-intensive tasks to compare direct System One decisions with explicit System Two reasoning under matched task conditions. Beyond task performance, we examine decision reliability under changes to the available options. Specifically, we test whether models maintain consistent decisions when options are reordered and recognize the absence of valid answer when the correct option is removed. These two aspects are combined into separate reliability score, allowing us to assess whether strong capability performance is accompanied by reliable decision-making. We evaluate 21 models on SO-Arena in terms of capability, inference latency, and decision reliability. The two System Two references lead the capability leaderboard, while GLiDE [28] and KnowLine-31B [67] achieve the highest scores among System One models, illustrating the remaining performance gap despite the latters substantial speed advantage. Reliability, however, does not follow the same ranking: JevAny-27B [86] achieves the highest reliability among the evaluated System One models despite ranking eleventh in capability. Beyond these aggregate results, we find that performance declines with increasing task difficulty, particularly in agentic settings, and that the benefits of stronger backbones and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce SO-Arena, comprising 2,919 tasks across 11 domains and five capability families. We establish traceable evaluation process and manually verify that reference labels are supported by the information available to the model. We introduce domain-specific difficulty tiers to distinguish model capabilities and extend evaluation beyond static judgments to interactive execution and history-dependent task verification. We develop separate reliability assessment combining decision consistency under option reordering and the ability to recognize missing correct answers, revealing aspects of decision-making overlooked by conventional accuracy metrics. We evaluate 21 models to reveal substantial capability differences across domains and difficulty levels, uneven benefits from model capacity and additional reasoning, and notable divergence between capability and reliability rankings. 2. Benchmark Design This section describes how we construct and evaluate our benchmark for System One decision-making. We first collect and derive tasks from public sources and control their quality (Section 3.1). We then organize these tasks by domain and, where applicable, difficulty tier, and formulate static and environmentbased tasks using common decision interface (Section 3.2). Given these task formulations, we define metrics for capability across domains and decision reliability (Section 3.3). Figure 3 summarizes the pipeline. 3.1. Data Sources and Quality Control We draw on 40 distinct public datasets, benchmarks, and environments across 11 domains. Representative sources include GoEmotions [24] for emotion understanding, MATH500 [54] for mathematics, GPQA Diamond [73] for scientific reasoning, Mind2Web [25] for web interaction, and BFCL [66] and ToolSandbox [57] for tool use. We convert the source data to our decision formats or derive new tasks from them, such as completion checks on BrowseComp-Plus [13] search runs and VirtualHome [71] trajectories. For quality control, we keep source labels as references, review them manually and with LLMs, and exclude items with questionable references. We record each tasks source, version, and original identifier where applicable, and flag model-derived references in the metadata. 4 SO-Arena Figure 3: Overview of SO-Arena. (1) Tasks are drawn or derived from 40 established public sources; items with questionable labels are dropped after human and LLM review. (2) The 2,919 tasks span 11 domains in five capability families, nine of which have domain-relative difficulty tiers, and are posed as static or environment-based tasks. (3) The capability score averages the hardest tier of each domain with equal domain weights, and the reliability score combines the option-reordering and missingcorrect-option tests. 3.2. Task Organization, Formulation, and Evaluation Settings We group the 11 domains into five capability families covering semantic understanding, knowledge and reasoning, safety and policy compliance, evidence assessment, and agent task completion. Of the 11 domains, nine have difficulty tiers. The remaining two, Sentiment & Emotion Understanding and Knowledge & Commonsense, are untiered because their tasks offer limited scope for systematically varying decision complexity. In the tiered domains, difficulty is relative to each domain and reflects the demands of its tasks. For example, Math uses source difficulty levels or the number of calculation steps, depending on the source. Task Completion Verification distinguishes direct state checks, judgments that require integrating evidence, and judgments that depend on the execution history. Figure 4(b) shows the distribution of tasks across tiers, and Appendix specifies the criteria for each tiered domain. To evaluate these capabilities in settings that reflect real-world applications, we consider how the context of task shapes the models decision. Some decisions can be made solely from fixed input, while others are made from the current state of an environment, such as website or sandbox with tools; in sequential tasks, each decision changes the state for the next, so later decisions depend on earlier ones being correct. We therefore organize the benchmark into two task settings, static and environment-based. Static Tasks. In static tasks, the model judges fixed input. We convert each source task into one of the three formats and keep the sources answer as the reference. For choice, multiple-choice questions are used as they are, and classification tasks offer the sources labels as options. Open-answer math problems have no options, so we build distractors from wrong answers of base model, intermediate results of the solution, and rule-based near misses. For noul, binary judgments are posed as yes/no questions, and multi-label task becomes one yes/no question per candidate label. For score, ordinal ratings keep the sources native scale. For tasks we build ourselves, we establish the reference by execution, verified construction, or annotation (Appendix A). We exclude tasks that require free-text responses. 5 SO-Arena (a) Families and domains (b) Difficulty tiers within each domain Figure 4: Composition of the benchmark. (a) Natural tasks by capability family (inner ring) and domain (outer ring). (b) Share of each domains tasks in each difficulty tier, with task counts on the bars; side rules mark the families in (a). Tiers are defined within each domain and are not calibrated across domains. Environment-Based Tasks. In environment-based tasks, the model assesses or selects actions given task goal and an observation from web or tool environment. Single-step web tasks show one recorded page state, on which the model judges whether proposed action advances the goal or selects the best candidate action. Sequential tasks require series of decisions, each choice from menu of candidate actions. In multi-step web tasks, the model acts at successive recorded states along reference route that replay has verified to complete the task.1 In interactive tool-use episodes, the BFCL [66] or ToolSandbox [57] simulator executes each selected action and returns the observation on which the next decision is made. We score each episode based on the corresponding benchmarks success criteria (Appendix A.6). The resulting benchmark comprises 2,300 static tasks and 619 environment-based tasks. The latter include 337 web tasks (100 single-step judgments and 237 reference-route tasks) and 282 interactive tooluse episodes. Related Work System One Models and Decision Benchmarks. System One models expose predictions over explicitly specified outcomes, enabling classification, routing, scoring, and verification without open-ended text generation. Jev introduced this interface as general-purpose service [2], while open releases such as Kev and JevAny provide language-model-based implementations [65, 86]. Recent research investigates how these capabilities can be obtained from pretrained models: SII-Decision distills reasoning-informed predictions into single-pass readout, whereas Releasing the Inner Jev studies answer-token readout and supervised adaptation [26, 32]. Evaluation efforts already extend beyond accuracy. JevBench measures capability, calibration, latency, and cost [5]; JEVal covers ten application domains and examines how local decisions compose into agent workflows and social simulations [26]. OpenDecisions additionally includes difficulty tiers and controlled perturbations [32]. Our work complements these efforts with withindomain difficulty tiers, controlled history-dependent verification, and separate reliability score within broader evaluation of decision competence. SO-Arena Generalist Capability Evaluation. MMLU measures knowledge and problem solving across academic and professional subjects [39], while BIG-Bench Hard probes challenging tasks and the effects of explicit reasoning [78]. Humanitys Last Exam extends evaluation toward expert-level academic questions [10]. These benchmarks establish useful measures of capability breadth and demanding problem solving. HELM further emphasizes standardized evaluation across scenarios and multiple desiderata, including calibration and efficiency [53]. SO-Arena adopts complementary focus: assessing generalist competence through decisions over supplied evidence and specified alternatives, while also examining whether judgments remain reliable as their informational and temporal requirements change. Academic reasoning is therefore one component of our evaluation, alongside semantic, policy, evidence, and environment-dependent decisions. Judges, Reward Models, and Verification Reliability. Research on LLM-as-a-judge establishes the usefulness of automated evaluation while documenting position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases [93]. RewardBench evaluates preferences across chat, safety, and reasoning, whereas JudgeBench constructs response comparisons grounded in factual and logical correctness [47, 80]. VerifyBench examines agreement between candidate responses and reference answers across scientific domains, including sensitivity to response presentation [52]. These studies motivate scrutinizing the evaluator itself. Separately, calibration research distinguishes predictive accuracy from the quality of confidence estimates, and selective classification studies the trade-off between error and coverage [30, 36]. We connect these perspectives to general-purpose decision evaluation, encompassing judgments whose evidence consists of documents, structured states, or interaction histories rather than only candidate answer pairs. Evaluation in Agentic Environments. Mind2Web evaluates action prediction across tasks, websites, and domains [25]. WebArena provides reproducible web environments and functional evaluation using answers and programmatic state checks [94]; τ-bench evaluates policy-constrained tool interaction using database outcomes and repeated-trial reliability [89]. More recently, VerifierBench evaluates the generation of executable checkers against valid solutions, ordinary errors, and adversarial cases [90]. These works address complementary evaluation targets: executing tasks, maintaining reliable behavior, or constructing verification programs. We evaluate decision models in two of these roles: as the policy that chooses each action of tool or web episode from menu of public options, and as the verifier that judges recorded executions, including trajectories whose final goal projections agree while their histories differ (Appendix A.4). 6. Conclusion We introduce SO-Arena, benchmark assessing generalist competence and decision reliability in System One models across eleven domains. It combines difficulty-stratified tasks, action selection and completion verification, and controlled option-set interventions to evaluate performance beyond aggregate accuracy. Our evaluation of 21 models reveals substantial capability gaps on demanding tasks, especially in agentic settings, despite the latency advantages of System One models. Stronger backbones and additional reasoning offer domain-dependent gains rather than universal improvements. More importantly, strong competence does not guarantee reliable judgment: option-order stability largely tracks performance, while recognition of missing correct options varies considerably among similarly capable models. These findings highlight the need to advance both capability and reliability in future System One models.

Semantic Understanding Sentiment & Emotion Understanding (200). We construct 200 items from five public datasets. From the All Beauty category of Amazon Reviews 2023 [42], we sample 50 reviews, with 10 for each recorded star rating. We sample 40 single-label test comments from GoEmotions [24], with four per target emotion across ten emotions. We also construct 30 aspect-level sentiment items from 10 restaurant sentences in ARTS [88]. The items use two decision formats. In ordinal score items, the model reads review title and text and predicts the reviewers rating on the original 15 star scale. In single-label classification items, the model selects one label from shuffled list of options. GoEmotions items use the full set of 28 labels, including labels outside the ten emotions used for sampling. We score predictions against the recorded star rating or the source label, depending on the format. SO-Arena Intent & Routing (300). We construct 300 items, with 100 per difficulty tier. For the easy tier, we sample 42 single requests from CLINC150 [48], 40 from BANKING77 [8], and 18 from SGD [72]. For the medium tier, we select 100 complete NatCS [35] customer-service conversations (36 insurance, 30 banking, and 34 finance). The audits set aside 30 medium and 20 hard candidates because of label uncertainty or poor task fit. The tiers differ in what the model must identify. Easy items ask the model to judge the intent of single request. Medium items require tracking exactly two customer goals across full conversation. The goals may appear far apart, and the model must distinguish them from goals suggested only by the agent. Hard items require identifying which components of larger domain ontology apply to an utterance. The easy tier uses 47 four-way choice items and 53 binary noul items. Each choice item presents the native intent and three neighboring native classes, while each noul item asks whether one candidate intent applies. In the medium tier, we pose one noul question per native goal label, yielding 2239 questions per conversation. In the hard tier, we pose one noul question per ontology component, yielding 48 questions for banking and 40 for hotels. We use the native component definitions verbatim. For medium and hard items, we form the predicted label set from all labels whose affirmative probability exceeds 0.5. We construct 500 items from six sources, drawing 150 from RAGTruth [59], 75 from ReasoningShield [49], 50 from HarmThoughts [45], 100 from DynaBench [41], 100 from Aegis 2.0 [33], and 25 from the hard-benign subset of OR-Bench [22]. In RAGTruth, the model either judges whether response contains hallucination relative to the supplied material (90 items) or identifies which segment, if any, contains the sole hallucinated span (60). DynaBench items ask either whether dialogue complies with given policy (50) or which 23 SO-Arena rule, if any, it violates (50). Aegis items assess prompt safety (50) or response safety (50), and OR-Bench items test over-refusal on hard benign prompts. We score each decision against its reference label. Of the 500 references, 100 are model-derived, comprising 50 original HarmThoughts LLM annotations, 25 Aegis response labels from an LLM jury, and 25 OR-Bench labels based on hard-benign subset membership. We append an executable sequence, called the audit suffix, that changes appliance states, removes two target objects, and restores zero, one, or both. trajectory can therefore end with the objects in their required positions even if they were misplaced when an appliance was operated. The model judges three conditions. C1 requires at least one switch-on in the suffix and checks that all required object placements hold immediately before every such action. C2 requires at least one close action in the suffix and checks that all required placements hold immediately before the first close. C3 checks whether all original state and placement goals hold after the last action. The model selects one of four three-bit profiles, and each distractor flips exactly one bit of the correct profile. For each base task, we generate and verify all eight profiles, retaining four for evaluation and four as counterfactual witnesses. For every evaluated trajectory, verified counterfactual reaches the same final goal state while changing the value of C1 or C2. Each condition is true in 10 of the 20 evaluated items. We use the verified profiles as references for the hard items and new model-derived annotations as references for the BrowseComp-Plus items. For evidence-sufficiency questions, negative answer indicates that the visible evidence is insufficient to establish the requirement. We use the base task as the resampling unit when estimating uncertainty for the 20 hard items. 24 A.5. Agent Task Completion SO-Arena Tool & API Use (282). We construct 282 episodes from 204 BFCL [66] requests and 78 ToolSandbox [56] scenarios. The easy tier contains 100 BFCL requests that specify an operation explicitly or require direct lookup. Of these, 26 start at the first turn and 74 start at later turn. The medium tier contains all 78 ToolSandbox scenarios, each presented as single self-contained request. The hard tier contains 104 original first-turn requests from multi-turn BFCL tasks. Across the tier, these requests involve dependent lookups, conditional actions, or several coordinated outcomes. For episodes that start partway through an interaction, we replay the earlier BFCL turns or execute the earlier ToolSandbox turns in the simulator and show the resulting history to the model. We automatically resolve decisions with single available option. Each episode has separate budgets for model decisions and native tool calls, with limits of 96 decisions and 12 calls for hard BFCL tasks. Tool calls that exceed time, memory, or output limits return an error and have no effect. Appendix A.6 describes how the episodes are scored. Text-based Web Interaction (337). We construct 337 items from 100 single steps of Mind2Web [25] demonstrations and 237 BreakingWeb [91] tasks across seven simulated applications. The Mind2Web steps form the easy tier and test whether the model can identify the relevant page element given the operation and any text to enter. The medium and hard tiers contain 137 and 100 BreakingWeb tasks, with 361 and 969 scored decisions, respectively. To enter the hard tier, task must have at least five scored decisions or at least three entity choices whose targets are not named in the instruction. It must also include at least one decision that requires recalling value from an earlier page, choosing from menu with more than 60 options, or inferring several entities. In the easy tier, 50 items ask whether supplied action advances the goal and 50 ask the model to select the best of four actions, using other controls on the same page as distractors. In the medium and hard tiers, the model makes decisions about which entity to act on, what exact value to enter, and when to stop. To fill field, the model first selects the field, then selects group if there are more than 64 candidate values, and finally selects the exact text span to enter. Reference routes are found by an external LLM or written by hand, and we replay each route to successful completion under the original checker. We also accept alternative action orders and detours when replay confirms that the task can still be completed. A.6. Scoring of Tool-Use Episodes Each tool-use episode is scored by the checker of its source benchmark. BFCL. An episode scores 1 if BFCLs multi-turn checker accepts it and 0 otherwise. The checker compares the state of the simulated backend and the results of the models tool calls with those of the reference calls [66]. ToolSandbox. ToolSandbox specifies each scenario by milestones, events that must occur in order, and minefields, events that must not occur. Its native score measures how closely the episode matches the milestones and is 0 if any minefield occurs [56]. We make two adaptations. We omit the wording checks on final acknowledgements, because our interface accepts only structured decisions, and we award score of 1 whenever the full goal state is reached without minefield violation.
